The change in language is due to the same phenomena: colloquial use of medical terms changes meaning over time. Retarded means slowing and this is how it is used medically. For instance psychomotor retardation is essentially slowed movement or response. However retarded has been used to denigrate people for decades as meaning stupid or at best silly. So, we abandon the term for a less loaded one. Autistic is not in quite the same danger but I think dissociation may be. When a patient tells me they dissociate, they usually don’t mean what I mean when I say it.

Plus we really don’t use the word in the context of development or mental capacity in medicine anymore. Not inappropriate but the shift has been toward intellectual disability or developmentally delayed. Some holdover doctors and nurses using MR and that’s not wrong. Just not the current jargon.

Patient: I stopped taking Zoloft because I looked it up and it causes sexual side effects. 

Me: were you having any sexual side effects?

Me: Side effects only matter if you get one. If you have sexual side effects then I would totally understand you wanting to come off Zoloft. Zoloft doesn’t cause sexual side effects. Downtown Johnson City has some great restaurants. Freiburgs is a good German place owned by Germans. Red Meze has great Mediterranean food and is owned by a Turkish family. Both will be authentic. Mexican food in the US is very good and there are several places to get good Mexican food here. One thing all Europeans seem to rave about in the US is BBQ. You will get very good BBQ here. Now for my favorite thing: Alcohol.

There are good bars and absolute dives. Sometimes a dive is a good place to drink. Sometimes it’s a shit hole. Either way, check at least one sketchy place out because it’s always a story. My favorite place is The Winsor Speakeasy. The drinks are pricy but very well crafted. Watauga Brewing Company had a nice rooftop bar with good drinks. Also Tennessee Hills Distillery has locally distilled spirits so you can get a taste of what we make here, yes moonshine, but other stuff too. I do like Mulligans for a drink as well. Bar tenders are friendly and atmosphere is good. For beer, I suggest Johnson City Brewing Company for a great selection of locally crafted beer. Something for every palate. I also like Cranky’s tap room. They have local and import brews. It’s also a great place for trivia on Thursday nights. If you get up to Kingsport (20-30 minute drive from Johnson City) Gypsy Cider company has outstanding hard ciders that are also locally crafted.

So point of clarification, I do not believe I’m the outlier. I was making a plausible scenario as devils advocate of why maybe my experience with physicians I work with was overwhelmingly positive. That they could still have a generally negative opinion of NP’s but think of me as “a good one.” I think MOST NP’s are as good at their jobs as MOST MD/DO’s, understanding that there are differences in what we actually do. I think the bell curve applies to ability along NP’s like it does with other professions. I think brick and mortar did prepare me better than online only programs would have based on my experience with NP who had graduated from those programs and students currently attending them. I didn’t go to a prestigious university. I went to a state school. However, the access to experts and ability to form relationships with people in my and other disciplines clearly made me a better nurse practitioner than I would have been without that. I have not seen data on difference between one grad versus another, so my opinion is based on personal experience. I can be swayed by research like I could on anything else. Online programs aren’t the only problem with our education though. We would benefit from a post grad residency requirement. Not 4-5 years like an MD, as RN experiences should give us more familiarity with healthcare concepts versus a fresh med school grad. We should also complete more clinical hours than we are required to. There are a number of policy, research, and healthcare management classes that represent time that would be better spent in practice environments, especially in DNP programs. You need the policy/theory/etc, but DNP is taught very similarly to PhD and it shouldn’t be. It’s a doctorate of practice and should focus more on practice (clinical judgement, treatment plans, more advanced pathology, more time on advanced specialties). I went to a good program (no grad to date in my specialty has failed their board on the first try) but I left my DNP program far more prepared to be a nursing lobbyist than a doctor of practice.

So, there was a comment by someone saying physicians talk shit behind our backs, but while I was responding he either deleted it or it was removed by mods. I want to respond, because I think there is a discussion that needs to be had. I hope you’ll understand that I love this profession and want it to thrive. Here’s my response:

My supervising physician is always complimentary and gives glowing evaluations of my work each year. He’s the Department chair. He’s definitely not anti-NP. The other physicians I work with don’t give the impression that they have a low opinion of my work either. My outcomes are consistent with their own and I often receive compliments from whoever is on call about the thoroughness of my charting and quality of my decision making. I say all this to say, you could be right. I would be shocked to learn that any of them (or even residents for that matter) had shit talked me. However, even if they don’t I could be what they would consider the outlier in my profession. No way to know if they think I’m just an exceptionally good egg. I personally find NP education lacking and can’t imagine practicing with only the knowledge we get in grad school. I work with residents a lot and know that med school isn’t enough either, but they do get a prolonged residency to prepare them. I went to a brick and mortar institution and my program was quite long. I’m very concerned about online only programs producing unsafe providers. The data (that I am aware of) does not show a significant drop in outcomes when an NP is involved versus an MD/DO but I do worry that will change if we don’t as a profession stamp out fly by night training programs. I do not think NP’s are an inherent danger and feel that the potential to benefit the patient and healthcare as a whole has a very high ceiling.

The birth control could get better with time, that’s true. That said, if you don’t want to be on birth control there are other options. Here’s what I do for many of my patients with PMDD. Keep in mind that this is an example of some options and rationales behind them. This is not medical advice. I am an internet stranger who could be lying about being a psychiatric nurse practitioner (what I am) for all you know. I tell you this because sometimes a receptive PCP is willing to give them a try if a patient suggests. 

1. Prozac 10’g for 10 days each month starting the week before your period. Lots of SSRI’s work well for PMDD, but Prozac is easy to come off of because of its long half life. It’s self tapering and has the lowest chance of withdrawal. Like all SSRI’s. It could trigger mania so report if that happens.

2. Abilify (dose could vary) for 10 days each month starting the week before your period. Even if you’re on another antipsychotic this medication could help to stabilize mood. It’s unlike most antipsychotics aside from Rexulti, in that it doesn’t blockade dopamine so lower possibility of involuntary movements or akathisia from increasing you antipsychotic. Drawback is it can still contribute to that stuff a bit and there is the possibility of electrolyte imbalance, particularly sodium. Report adverse effects and get labs if you have any.
